questions.q: Per this lesson, what distinguishes an experienced developer's approach to debugging from a frustrating, random hunt?
options: Experienced developers treat debugging as a repeatable process and trust that method more than their assumptions about what the code should be doing
Experienced developers simply have more innate talent that beginners lack
Experienced developers never encounter unexpected behavior in their code
Experienced developers always rewrite the entire program from scratch when something breaks
questions.explain: The lesson's central claim is that the difference isn't talent -- it's having and trusting a repeatable method, rather than treating debugging as random luck.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call the 'shotgun' approach of randomly changing lines of code risky?
options: It is always slower than the systematic process with no exceptions
It always causes a compile-time error
Apex specifically forbids making more than one code change at a time
It sometimes accidentally works but teaches you nothing about why, and can introduce a second bug while chasing the first
questions.explain: The lesson warns that randomly changing code might coincidentally fix the symptom without revealing the actual cause, and risks introducing new bugs in the process -- which is why it recommends a systematic process instead.

questions.q: What are the four steps of the systematic debugging process this lesson describes, in order?
options: Guess, fix, test, deploy
Reproduce it reliably, isolate it, form a hypothesis, verify it
Isolate, reproduce, fix, verify
Hypothesize, reproduce, deploy, isolate
questions.explain: The lesson lists the process in this exact order: first find reliable repro steps, then narrow down the responsible code, then state a specific checkable hypothesis, then verify it's correct before writing the fix.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes 'I think discountRate is holding 10 instead of 0.1 by the time it reaches this calculation' a good hypothesis, compared to 'something's broken'?
options: It uses more words, which always makes a hypothesis stronger
It guarantees the bug will be fixed immediately
It is specific and checkable -- it names exactly what is believed to be wrong, in a way that can be verified with a debug statement before changing any code
It avoids using the word 'Integer'
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct contrast between a vague claim ('something's broken') and a specific, checkable hypothesis naming the exact suspected problem -- which is what makes step 3 of the process useful rather than just another guess.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat the phrase 'this should work' as a warning sign rather than a conclusion?
options: Because it is grammatically incorrect
Because it means the code definitely has a compile-time error
Because Apex automatically flags this phrase as an error
Because it signals reasoning from an assumption about the code rather than evidence from actually running and observing it -- exactly the moment right before discovering it doesn't work
questions.explain: The lesson explains that 'it should work' reflects reasoning from assumption rather than observed evidence, and that the fix is always to stop assuming and go look at what the code is actually doing, line by line.
